what.early: American Indians the census counted. Before 1890 it left out "Indians not taxed" (those living on reservations or in tribal territory, most Native people), so these counts are far too low.
what.full: American Indians, the first census to count Native people on reservations and in Indian Territory too (a special Indian census added to the regular count).
what.race: American Indian (from 1960 also Eskimo and Aleut), counted by the census.
what.alone: American Indian and Alaska Native alone (people who gave one race). Counting everyone who named it alone or with another race roughly doubles it from 2000 on (9.7 million in 2020).

estimates.source: Sherburne F. Cook, The Population of the California Indians, 1769-1970 (University of California Press, 1976); A. L. Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925) for the low figure of 133,000
estimates.note: The range is between scholars, not a margin of error: Kroeber's 133,000 (1925) and Cook's revised 310,000 (1976) for the eve of the Spanish missions. Some scholars think epidemics reached California before 1769, which would make both too low for 1492. In the 1833 epidemic alone at least 20,000 people died in the Central Valley (Cook, The Epidemic of 1830-1833 in California and Oregon, 1955, p. 322).

estimates.source: Benjamin Madley, An American Genocide: The United States and the California Indian Catastrophe, 1846-1873 (Yale University Press, 2016); Cook's figure for 1845
estimates.note: Madley: between 1846 and 1873 California's Native population fell from perhaps 150,000 to 30,000. Gary Clayton Anderson thinks Cook's 1845 figure may be too high.
The 1880 census counted 16,277 American Indians in California, but before 1890 the census left out Indians it did not tax, so the count is too low to compare.

estimates.label: 1.9–7+ million
estimates.source: Douglas H. Ubelaker, North American Indian population size, A.D. 1500 to 1985, American Journal of Physical Anthropology 77 (1988): 289-294 (1,894,350); Russell Thornton, American Indian Holocaust and Survival (University of Oklahoma Press, 1987) (7+ million, over 5 million in the present-day United States), both as reported in National Research Council, America Becoming, vol. 1 (2001), ch. 5
estimates.note: North of Mexico, about 1500. The estimates differ by method: Ubelaker adds up tribe-by-tribe figures; Thornton allows for epidemics before any written count.

estimates.source: Russell Thornton, American Indian Holocaust and Survival (1987), as cited in J. David Hacker and Michael R. Haines, American Indian Mortality in the Late Nineteenth Century, NBER Working Paper 12572 (2006)
estimates.note: The area of today's United States in 1800, not the United States of 1800.
